paper_title: AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As the production of software passes into the hands of software itself, coding agents are increasingly commissioned to build agents fitted to their users' own workflows. This delegation carries a quiet assumption, that the delivered agent will faithfully serve the requirement it was built for, rather than merely appear to. No existing benchmark tests that assumption. We introduce AgentSWE, a benchmark for agent software engineering spanning three stages of the agent development lifecycle: Creation of a complete agent from a natural-language requirement, Editing of production agent codebases, and Optimization toward a measurable target. Each of its 25 tasks is framed as a commission rather than an exam: the builder iterates against a handful of illustrative cases, while acceptance exercises the frozen submission on held-out cases designed to span the full requirement, grading behavior against requirement-derived rubrics under hard pass/fail gates or, for Optimization, against the source benchmark's own objective. Evaluating a range of coding agents across models and harnesses, we find that none comes close to delivering what a requirement asks for: the gap between what a builder demonstrates and what it delivers is the norm, not the corner case. An accompanying empirical analysis of the failure trajectories identifies recurring failure modes, among them overfitting to the visible cases, hollow runtimes behind code that looks complete, and unsupported claims of completion, each a signal by which coding agents can learn to build the agents they are asked for.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Coding agents such as Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026) and Codex (OpenAI, 2026a) now carry substantial engineering workloads (Chen et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025b), and many of their users are not engineers: they describe what they need and delegate the rest (Hitzig et al., 2026). Increasingly, what they delegate is the building of an agent, program that wraps model, tools, and state around one recurring job so that the job runs on fixed runtime, at fixed cost, without coding agent attending each run. Delegation of this kind rests on trust: that coding agent, handed requirement in natural language, will deliver the agent its user intends rather than one that merely appears to comply. Whether that trust is warranted is what this paper measures. Agent development spans three stages. It begins with creation, where natural-language requirement must become working system; continues through editing, where new capabilities join living codebase without unsettling what already works; and matures into optimization, where the agent is pushed toward an explicit target, be it public leaderboard or production workload. Handing this lifecycle to coding agents invites failures subtler than broken code: an agent that passes visible examples yet misses the intent behind them (Liu et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2026a; Lodkaew et al., 2026); tool registered but never invoked (Soni, 2026; Fan et al., 2026); goal that drifts over long horizon (Arike et al., 2025; Menon et al., 2026); report citing evidence no source contains (Onweller et al., 2026; Rao et al., 2026). Such failures are not hypothetical; they are the present condition of Equal contribution. Corresponding author.

The questions are how far coding agents compromise the requirements they are handed, on which capabilities, and for what reasons. These questions outrun the instruments we have. SWE-bench and its descendants grade the repair of conventional software against reference patch or test suite (Jimenez et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2024); NL2Repo-Bench commissions whole repositories from requirement documents (Ding et al., 2025); Paper2Code and PaperBench rebuild research implementations checked against the papers they reproduce (Seo et al., 2025; Starace et al., 2025). Each judges ordinary code against an answer known in advance. commissioned agent wraps stochastic policy around tools, answers to requirement that has no reference solution, and keeps changing after delivery. Benchmarks that do evaluate agents, from AgentBench onward (Liu et al., 2024), examine finished agent and ask how well it performs; none asks whether coding agent could have built it. Work on agents that design or improve other agents (Hu et al., 2025; Mishra et al., 2026) comes closest, but it measures how far search procedure or meta-agent can raise benchmark score, not whether general coding agent delivers the agent requirement describes (Section 2). Between judging built software and judging finished agents lies step that current suites leave unmeasured: building the agent that requirement asks for. We introduce AgentSWE, benchmark that turns faithful delegation from anecdote into measurement (Figure 1) through three commitments. The first is to measure the whole lifecycle, through twenty-five tasks spanning all three stages. Ten Creation tasks commission complete agent from naturallanguage requirement, over workloads from GUI automation to formal theorem proving, each scoped against mature open-source system; ten Editing tasks ask for new capabilities in the pinned codebase of production agent such as OpenHands or Aider, capabilities that cut through crash recovery, permission fencing, and transactional state; and five Optimization tasks set working agent against measurable target. The second commitment is that evaluation should mirror the delegation it studies. Each task is framed as commission: the builder sees only what customer could provide, while acceptance also tests the stated clauses its examples leave out. The builder develops against the requirement and few illustrative cases; held-out cases then test the frozen delivery in isolation. The third commitment follows from the absence of prescribed reference implementation: every Creation and Editing execution is graded against rubric derived from the requirement itself, and hard gates assign zero to invalid executions and inapplicable patches. We put this instrument to work on five models as builders in the Codex harness, together with further pairings of harness and model. The verdict is sobering. The strongest builders average 19.1 on Creation and 31.6 on Editing, and in Optimization no builder closes more than 5 % of the remaining gap to the target on average, and only 13 of the 25 runs score above their starter. Builders overfit to the visible development cases, and the delivery fails on the clauses those cases leave out; they ship hollow runtimes, code that reads as complete but does no work when run; and both builders and the agents they deliver claim completions that their own records contradict. Each of these modes names habit that the next generation of coding agents can be built and trained to avoid. More development cases, prescribed design, an instruction to test, and longer case budget shift the scores but leave held-out Result low under every condition. In sum, this paper makes three contributions. First, we formalize agent software engineering as measurable problem, in which builder must satisfy requirement it can probe only through limited development feedback. Second, we deliver AgentSWE, twenty-five commissions whose acceptance executes the delivered agent on held-out cases and grades each run with requirement-derived rubric or native objective, and we evaluate various harnessmodel pairings against it. Third, we contribute an empirical analysis of the failure trajectories, which identifies recurring failure modes of coding agents and turns each into direction for the next generation of coding agents.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Agents that build and optimize agents. Research on automated agent development has expanded both the scope of what can be designed and the stage at which adaptation occurs. Early approaches generate task-specific roles, tools, and collaboration patterns from task descriptions or seed agents (Chen et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026). Subsequent work formulates agent development as optimization, first over textual components such as instructions and demonstrations (Yang et al., 2024a; Khattab et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2025), and then over broader design spaces containing agent modules, communication structures, and executable workflows (Zhuge et al., 2024; Shang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025c;a; Zhou et al., 2025). This paradigm has further expanded to searching over complete code-defined agents and multi-agent scaffolds (Hu et al., 2025; Rosser & Foerster, 2025). related line relaxes the assumption that the improvement procedure itself remains fixed. Initial systems support self-referential modification of an improver or agent logic (Zelikman et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2025), while later approaches expose complete implementations, harnesses, and meta-level improvement mechanisms to revision (Robeyns et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026b; Lee et al., 2026; Hebbar et al., 2026). Arbor (Jin et al., 2026) carries hypotheses and evidence across long-horizon artifact optimization, whereas JIT-Agent (Zhang et al., 2026a) synthesizes task-conditioned executable harnesses at inference time. Together, these developments establish agent construction and optimization as capability in its own right. AgentSWE makes this capability the object of evaluation, measuring whether general-purpose coding agents can create, modify, and optimize agents from heterogeneous user requirements. Benchmarks for agent construction. Most agent benchmarks hold the agent implementation fixed and evaluate its performance within given environment. Recent benchmarks move beyond task completion by asking agents to construct or iteratively improve more complex artifacts. WorFBench (Qiao et al., 2025) evaluates generated workflow structures, while benchmarks for machine-learning experimentation and research engineering evaluate improvement of executable research artifacts (Huang et al., 2024; Nathani et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025). AI4AI-Bench (Chi et al., 2026) extends this setting to the redesign of model-training algorithms. Other evaluations isolate specific improvement mechanisms: SE-Bench (Yuan et al., 2026) studies knowledge internalization, whereas OPT-BENCH (Li et al., 2026) measures feedback-driven solution refinement. These benchmarks evaluate workflows, research artifacts, or optimized solutions rather than deployable agents. Closest to our setting, AIE-Bench (Mishra et al., 2026) evaluates whether meta-agent can improve pinned target-agent scaffold under controlled mutation boundaries and trial budgets. AgentSWE extends this setting to the full agent-development lifecycle: creating agents from natural-language commissions, modifying existing agent codebases without regression and optimizing working agents toward measurable objectives. By freezing submissions and evaluating their behavior on held-out cases, AgentSWE measures whether coding agents can deliver the agents users actually request.

sections.title: 4 THE AGENTSWE BENCHMARK
sections.content: AgentSWE turns Definition 3.1 into 25 commissions: ten Creation, ten Editing, and five Optimization tasks. Each task hands coding agent, the builder, requirement q, an initial artifact a0, and development cases D, and grades the agent it delivers on held-out cases. Figures 2 and 3 show how tasks are built and evaluated; Section walks through one task per family. 4.1 TASK CONSTRUCTION Each family fixes the requirement and the initial artifact a0 in its own way (Figure 2a). In every family, GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026c) drafts the task materials from the analyzed source system, and the authors verify and refine each draft. Creation tasks come from open-source domain agents on GitHub, in domains from desktop automation and scientific PDF translation to formal theorem proving. Each repository is reverse-engineered into self-contained goal and set of functional requirements, extended with capabilities that broaden its purpose and raise the compositional difficulty,

sections.title: 4.2 TASK PACKAGE
sections.content: Each task separates what the builder sees, namely q, a0, and the development cases D, from what evaluation reserves (Figure 2b). Every Creation and Editing task publishes two development cases, which demonstrate the entry point, the delivery contract, and small part of the required functionality; Optimization draws development split from the instance pool of its source benchmark. Evaluation reserves the held-out cases and the scoring contract. Each Creation and Editing task holds out six cases. Each case exercises one or more requirement clauses, among them clauses and capability interactions that the requirement states but the development cases leave out, and together the six cover diverse inputs, state, and data. Optimization holds out disjoint split of the same pool. In total the suite has 150 development and 365 held-out cases. The scoring contract of Creation or Editing task is task-specific Result rubric whose weighted items derive from the functional requirements, with gates and ceilings for violations of the interface contract and the constraints (Section C); Optimization keeps the native evaluator of its source benchmark. Held-out inputs, evaluator state, scoring contracts, credentials, and model routing never enter the builders workspace, and the builder receives feedback only on its development cases. 4.3 EVALUATION PROTOCOL Development and freezing. Harbor (Harbor Framework Team, 2026), container framework for agent evaluation, runs the builder in one persistent session (Figure 3, left). The builder works in private writable workspace and may submit snapshot of its delivery at any time. Each snapshot runs on the development cases in isolated jobs, and the scores and summarized feedback return to the same session, within fixed time and submission budgets (Section E). Development ends when the builder exits or exhausts its submissions or its time budget. Creation then freezes the workspace; Editing freezes the last accepted submission, so builder whose submissions were never accepted delivers nothing; Optimization freezes the accepted snapshot with the highest development objective. Freezing records the delivery and its software environment, and the held-out evaluation verifies that neither has changed. Held-out execution. Each held-out case runs the frozen delivery through its fixed entry point in an isolated, pinned runtime (Figure 3, right; Section D). Every model call the delivered agent makes goes through benchmark-owned gateway to one runtime model, shared by all deliveries in task family, so that the score reflects what the builder contributes: prompts, tool orchestration, context and state management, and output validation. Scoring. For Creation and Editing, deterministic gates first assign zero to an execution that does not launch, exceeds its time budget, or produces no parseable deliverable. frontier reasoning model at its highest effort then applies the Result rubric (Zheng et al., 2023; Arora et al., 2025) (GPT-5.6 Sol for Creation, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026b) for Editing; Table 9). The judge grades what the agent produced on one concrete case, its artifacts, execution trace, and resulting state, rather than the quality of its code, and ceilings bind the score to the violations the evaluator records. Optimization reports gap closure = 100γ (Equation (3)), computed from the change = J(ˆa) J(a0) in the native objective on the held-out split; is negative when the candidate scores below its starter. Section gives the settings for each task family; Section discusses the limitations of the evaluation. 5.2 HELD-OUT PERFORMANCE Creation success is rare and task-specific. The 50 Creation runs in Table 1 average Result of 11.2 (median 3.4), and 20 of them score zero. The highest-scoring builder, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, averages 19.1 yet scores below 20 on eight of ten tasks. Only three runs exceed 50, all on formal theorem proving or repository bug repair, and no builder exceeds 30 on more than one task. Success on one commission does not carry over to the next, and none of the evaluated builders reliably builds the agents that AgentSWE specifies. Editing yields partial capabilities, or no delivery at all. The builders that deliver on nearly every task, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.6 Sol, still realize only part of the commissioned capabilities: their means lie between 20 and 35, and only one run, GPT-5.5 on the Codex task, reaches 70. Qwen3.6 fails earlier: it submits no candidate on any task, typically ending its session right after announcing plan. DeepSeek-V4-Flash delivers on four tasks; on most of the others it works until the budget runs out without ever submitting candidate. Adding capabilities to working product thus fails in two ways: the patch covers only part of the requirement, or the builder never finishes one. Optimization gains are inconsistent across tasks. No builder closes more than 5 % of the remaining gap to the target on average. sections.title: 5.3 TRAJECTORY ANALYSIS AND FAILURE MODES
sections.content: Analyzing the builders trajectories, the frozen artifacts, and the delivered agents execution traces in the main runs, we find three recurring failure modes (Section gives the protocol). Overfitting to the visible cases. Development scores overstate what delivery does on the rest of the requirement, so the gap FD of Section 3.2 is wide. Eleven Creation runs end development with score of at least 90, yet their held-out Result averages 9.9; one of them hard-codes its two development cases (Section I). DeepSeek-V4-Pro Editing delivery scores 100 on development cases and 28.3 on held-out cases. In Optimization, the selected candidate gains 13.1 points on development cases but only 1.8 on held-out cases (Section G.4), although both splits come from one instance pool; on four of the five benchmarks the gains shrink or reverse (Figure 4). Trajectories and artifacts reveal case-specific implementations: builders fit their agents to the visible cases in 14 of 25 Optimization runs and 13 of the 33 Editing runs that deliver. On PinchBench, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro route tasks by keyword to playbooks for visible task categories, gaining 8.1 and 59.4 points on development cases and losing 15.2 and 15.1 on held-out cases (Section I). Delivered Editing agents overclaim at run time too: in 13 of the 33 runs that deliver, they report outcomes that their own effect logs or state contradict, and the OpenWiki delivery above declares its run complete.

sections.title: 5.4 DISCUSSION
sections.content: The failure modes of Section 5.3 come from single builds under one set of conditions. We change these conditions one at time, namely the number of development cases, prompt prior on how to build, the case budget, and the harness, and we also repeat the build under fixed conditions, to see how held-out Result and the failure modes respond (Section E.2). Scores rise from zero to two development cases, not beyond. Development cases are what builders overfit to (Section 5.3). On two Creation tasks, with three builder runs per condition, we give the builder zero, one, two, or four of them. Going from zero to two development cases raises mean Result by 34.3 points on PDF translation and by 29.3 on PPTX generation  (Table 2)  ; without any case, all three PDF deliveries score zero. Two further cases add nothing on PDF and lower PPTX from 33.5 to 15.2 (Figure 7). prescribed design lowers PPTX; self-testing narrows its spread. We also append one of two prompt priors to the builder instruction (Section D.1). sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: The same pairing delivers very different agents across builds. The main comparison and harness studies build each pairing once. On eight tasks from the three families, we build each of three builders three times under fixed conditions (Table 5; Section E.2). Builds of one pairing can lie far apart (Figure 8): GPT-5.6 Sol scores 32.8, 33.3, and 90.5 on DeepTutor, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 0.0, 33.3, and 56.8 on repository bug repair. No builder leads on every task, and Qwen3.6 averages at most 6.0 on any task. Overfitting recurs: two GPT-5.6 Sol builds of database analytics reach 99 on the development cases and 11.0 and 6.5 on held-out cases (Section 5.3). The repository provides these eight tasks and this configuration as AgentSWE-Lite, lower-cost entry point for evaluation.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced AgentSWE to measure whether coding agents deliver agents that serve their requirement on cases they have not seen. Current builders rarely do: in the main comparison, the strongest average 19.1 on Creation and 31.6 on Editing, and in Optimization none closes more than 5 % of the remaining gap to the target on average. The trajectories reveal recurring failures: builders fit the visible cases, ship runtimes that read as complete but do not work, and, like the agents they deliver, claim completions their own records contradict. These failure modes chart where coding agents need to improve; our future work will pursue harnesses that test against the requirement and verify completion claims, and training that rewards behavior on unseen cases. AI USE STATEMENT We used generative AI tools for three tasks. First, to construct the benchmark, we used Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol to synthesize task materials from the analyzed source systems (Section 4.1): the requirement documents, the development and held-out cases, and the task-specific Result rubrics. The authors designed each commission and reviewed and revised the generated materials. Second, AI agents assisted the trajectory analysis (Sections 5.3 and H) by labeling failure modes from builder trajectories, execution traces, and evaluator records; the authors reviewed the labels and the resulting counts. Third, we used AI assistants to aid and polish the writing of this paper. Coding agents and language models are also the object of study, acting as builders, runtime models, and judges (Sections and 5.1); this use is part of the method rather than assistance to the authors. We have reviewed all AI-assisted content and take full responsibility for the paper. ETHICS STATEMENT AgentSWE asks coding agents to build agents that execute code, access the web, and, in one Creation task, validate software vulnerabilities. All builder sessions and candidate executions run in isolated containers with pinned fixtures, and every model call passes through benchmark-owned gateway (Section D). The benchmark involves no human subjects. Its tasks derive from public repositories and public benchmarks, used under their licenses and terms. Our analysis documents how coding agents misreport their own work, which we regard as safety-relevant property of delegating software to them. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT Section 4 and Sections and describe the tasks, cases, and scoring. Sections and give the evaluation infrastructure, builder instructions, model versions, effort settings, and budgets. Section reports repeated runs and the variation of repeated evaluation, Section lists per-run results, and Sections and describe the analysis protocol and the traced cases. The benchmark, comprising the task packages, the development and held-out cases, the Creation and Editing rubrics and judge prompts, the evaluators, and the evaluation harness, is available at https://github.com/ VectorSpaceLab/AgentSWE. Where an upstream license does not permit redistribution, the repository fetches the pinned upstream commit instead of including it. The repository also provides the eight tasks and the configuration of Table 5 as AgentSWE-Lite.

B.1 CREATION: SCIENTIFIC PDF TRANSLATION The builder starts from an empty workspace and must deliver reusable translator with an offline viewer that reads in both directions.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Requirement four Markdown documents 01_task_goal.md Background Agent to Create Target Users Core Value Final Objective Non-Goals You must create an Interactive Scientific PDF Translation Agent. It receives one Markdown request that identifies one or more local scientific PDFs, source and target languages, translated-PDF display mode, and optional terminology assets. It produces faithful translated PDF plus self-contained local reading viewer that displays the source and translation side by side with geometry-based paragraph correspondence. 02_interface_and_delivery.md Environment Preparation Uniform Run Command Input Contract Output Directory and Repeated Runs Required Successful Output PDF Contract Alignment Artifact Viewer Interaction Contract run_report.json Exit Codes and Failure Reports Every case is invoked exactly as python run_agent.py -input <input.md> -output <output_dir> [. . . ] successful run must contain all of these paths: translated.pdf, alignment.json, run_report.json, viewer/index.html, styles.css, app.js, documents/source.pdf, documents/translated.pdf, and vendor/. The browser must make no external network request after the output directory has been generated. 03_requirements_and_constraints.md nine functional requirements: interpret the complete request inspect every page and recover reading order translate faithfully preserve scientific objects and associations produce readable translated PDF build geometry-grounded alignment build the local viewer validate before success degrade honestly; implementation constraints; observable evaluation boundary 04_resources.md Evaluator-owned model transport Environment Ownership Runtime Envelope Credentials Multimodal Responses API API and Retrieval Budgets Serper-Compatible Search Search/Scrape Tool Layer Network and Filesystem Wall-clock limit: 600 seconds per case, including translation and validation. Memory limit: 4 GiB per case. Generation is non-interactive. Development case dev_002 Thermal Barrier Imaging Note Translate source_mixed.pdf from English to Simplified Chinese for materials-science researchers. Apply glossary.csv as authoritative and create the complete interactive reading bundle. Source condition. The four-page PDF is mixed: pages 1, 2, and 4 contain native selectable text, while page 3 is an embedded scan with mild skew, faint type, plot, and the printed batch mark TB-17. Page 4 is landscape. Recover page 3 by OCR or visual analysis without inventing illegible characters. Translated PDF. Produce bilingual English-Simplified Chinese PDF with exactly four pages and the same portrait/portrait/portrait/landscape sequence. Within each prose region, place the English source first and its Chinese translation directly below. [. . . ] Follow every glossary target exactly. Preserve TB-17, coating code YSZ-8, instrument IRX-4, citation markers, signs, decimal precision, units, α = k/(ρcp), Fo = αt/L2, and equation numbers (1) and (2). Alignment and viewer. Align source paragraphs to the Chinese part of each bilingual target region, not to the duplicated English. Include OCR-derived page-3 paragraphs with honest confidence. Visibly distinguish low-confidence links in the viewer. Bidirectional activation must work on native page 2, scanned page 3, and rotated landscape page 4. The supplied assets are the complete authority. Make zero search or retrieval calls and add no scan disclaimer page. Scoring Result rubric with six dimensions: semantic completeness and terminology 35, fidelity of scientific objects and data 35, page and reading structure 12, alignment auditability 8, offline viewer 8, delivery integrity and accessibility 2; gates and ceilings as described in Section C. The frozen source is also graded once on the shared static rubric (Section G.1). The difficulty is compositional: correct translation still fails part of the commission if its alignment points to the duplicated English, or if the viewer cannot find the rendered region. sections.content: Requirement four Markdown documents and checkpoint schema 01_task_goal.md Task goal: cross-instance transactional effect delivery Extend the supplied OpenHands Agent Canvas repository with backend-scoped, versioned recovery ledger for conversation effects. The product must stay honest when two service instances or browser tabs share storage, process stops after any delivery stage, lease expires and moves to new runtime, or pause/resume/cancel races an old callback. The ledger is transactional outbox, not merely history snapshot. 02_interface_and_delivery.md Submission Frozen TypeScript adapter Recovery-aware conversation event dispatcher Durable cross-tab recovery sync coordinator Transactional workspace recovery reconciler Persistence, integrity, and migration Delivery and crash semantics Lease, ABA, event, and compaction semantics Least-privilege inspection and production seams Error contract for deterministic crash injection Submit exactly these top-level files: solution.patch: non-empty UTF-8 unified Git patch relative to the supplied repository that applies with git apply exactly once. edit_report.json [. . . ] run_report.json [. . . ] Reports are evidence, not assertions of correctness. the durable outbox state machine: 03_requirements_and_constraints.md functional requirements constraints verifiable hard requirements queued -> claimed -> applied -> Implement completed, with uncertain, blocked, and cancelled recovery outcomes. Persist every stage before continuing, and never infer callback success from callback return digest alone. [. . . ] Modify only src/api/conversation-service/**, src/api/runtime-service/**, src/api/recovery/**, src/stores/** [. . . ] Do not modify lockfiles, package/build configuration, benchmark cases, generated output, authentication, network policy, or unrelated product code. 04_resources.md Pinned runtime Prewarm and install Runtime and memory envelope Filesystem Development case dev_001 Converge an interrupted workspace and lossy history stream Resume this public practice conversation. chunk write response and transport pull response were both lost after the far side had already acted on them, the history channel echoes its own notices back, and the workspace has local-only and remote-only path to reconcile. Five outcomes are required, and they are scored independently. 1. Upload exactly the missing chunk, once, after re-probing what the remote side genuinely lacks. 2. Converge exactly once on the union of the local-only and remote-only paths: one durable remote commit, one local apply. 3. Retry the lost transport response from the same durable cursor, not from the advisory remote cursor. 4. Complete, bounded projection; no duplicate effect. No side effect runs twice, and the public workspace projection carries every published stage field and no path, digest, chunk identifier, tab or incarnation identity, or token. An empty projection is not safe projection. 5. Keep runtime-event discipline. delivery that carries the current owner, lease epoch, fencing token, run generation and expected revision is genuine: accept it [. . . ] delivery whose fencing token or lease epoch does not match the live authority must be suppressed [. . . ] Suppressing everything is not safe answer. Report what actually happened. Claiming an outcome the product did not reach scores worse than reporting it honestly as unmet. Scoring patch that does not apply scores zero. Otherwise the Result rubric scores task completion 35, recovery quality 25, durable consistency 20, honest reporting 10, and privacy and scope 10, from numbered outcomes with observed facts, satisfaction flags, and safety flags; unmet outcomes impose ceilings (Section reconstructs one recorded score). The commission pairs positive obligation to resume legitimate work with negative obligation to reject stale work; an agent that refuses every action fails both.

Strategy Scientific PDF translation ## Strategy prior: architecture for scientific PDF translation Treat the created system as geometry-preserving document translation pipeline, not as page-level text replacement. Preserve freedom in libraries and models, but make these architectural responsibilities explicit: 1. Analyze each page before translation. Render and parse it, identify native versus scanned content, recover reading order and layout regions, and classify prose, formulas, code, tables, figures, captions, footnotes, references, headers, and protected identifiers. Use OCR or visual recovery only where native extraction is inadequate, with confidence attached to recovered units. 2. Maintain an intermediate document model whose units carry source page, reading order, text, geometry, type, protection policy, and confidence. Translation should operate on coherent prose units while scientific objects and their associations remain explicitly protected. 3. Separate extraction, translation, and reconstruction. Batch or cache translation where useful, enforce glossary/protected-token constraints, and validate numbers, signs, units, citations, equations, identifiers, negation, and modality before placing target text back into the document. 4. Reconstruct adaptively within the original page geometry. Choose suitable fonts, script direction, line breaking, local reflow, and bilingual pairing. Preserve page count, dimensions, rotations, columns, object associations, and page-local reading order while avoiding clipping, overlap, and text painted across graphics. 5. Derive alignment from the same intermediate geometry used for reconstruction. Map meaningful source/target units with real page boxes, multiple anchors when unit splits, stable reading-order IDs, digests, status, and calibrated confidence. Do not invent decorative boxes or align against detached transcript. 6. Build the viewer as an offline projection of the PDF and alignment artifacts. Bundle the renderer locally; use the alignment geometry for overlays; support bidirectional pointer and keyboard activation, active/ARIA synchronization, counterpart scrolling, page identity, and visible uncertainty. 7. Validate in layers before success: parse and render every PDF page; compare page count/dimensions/rotation; check glyph coverage and protected-token survival; validate alignment schema, bounds, order, digests, and visible overlap; then run clean-browser offline interaction smoke at both required viewports. 8. Recover honestly. Retry bounded OCR/translation/layout operations, isolate page-local failures, preserve uncertain visible tokens, lower confidence when warranted, and never silently omit page or fabricate an alignment. The reusable pattern is page analysis -> typed geometry model -> constrained translation -> adaptive reconstruction -> geometry-derived alignment -> offline viewer -> parse/render/browser validation and targeted repair. sections.content: Cases 14 each trace one failure from feedback or runtime actions to the frozen artifact or the observed state; case 5 traces repair that reaches the delivered agent. Quoted text is verbatim with omissions marked; structured records are condensed to the relevant fields. 1. development score built on two hard-coded cases. Qwen3.6s Database analytics delivery is single script of 2,073 lines that describes itself as pure Python stdlib, no external dependencies and never calls the runtime model. It classifies each request by phrases taken from the two development cases and dispatches to queries written for them: Case type: "commerce" if the request contains recognized net sales, decline by market, [. . . ]; "adoption" if it contains adoption, active_organization, [. . . ]; otherwise none. Queries: _build_commerce_q1_sql [. . . ] _build_adoption_q3_sql, with the quarter bounds and the refund cutoff written in as constants. Its development means climb from 38 to 99 over ten rounds and end at 96. The final feedback already points at the hard-coding: Round 10, dev 001 (92/100): dashboard.html switches between literal Harbor/Mesa panels instead of deriving the selected rows, total, and largest negative category from submitted result data [. . . ] The held-out requests ask for other analyses over other databases. Five of them exit after 0.01 with Unknown case type: None, the sixth with no such table: organizations, and all six fail the validity gate. 2. higher development mean hides displaced failures. DeepSeek-V4-Flashs PinchBench run M09 adds playbooks for task categories and routes tasks to them by keyword. Its own assessment of round 2 records the tradeoff: Round 2: 76.5 (up from 72.8) [. . . ] But regressions: meeting tldr (970), spreadsheet (995), contract (10062), syslog (3622). Later rounds fall to 60.6, 63.7, and 51.65, so round 2 is frozen. Its held-out mean is 40.625 against the starters 55.825, with 7 wins, 17 losses, and 16 ties. The higher development mean already contains large regressions on other visible tasks, and selection still favors it. 3. Cancellation succeeds, and late work still changes state. GPT-5.6 Sols OpenHands delivery runs pause, resume, and cancel on test_003. The product observations and the burst probe record: Lifecycle: pause generation 2; resume generation 3; cancel generation 4, cancellation revision 5. Burst after cancellation: 80 callbacks accepted, 0 rejected; audit length 1 81; revision 5 85; event cursor 0 3320; terminal state remains cancelled. The commission requires those late callbacks to change nothing. The terminal state is correct, and the suppression fails: the audit log and the revision counter grow with every accepted callback. The agents report acknowledges the burst. 4. final report describes discarded revision. The GPT-5.5 OSWorld run M20 selects round 3 (dev 40) after later rounds score 20 and 30. Its final report nevertheless describes harness changes: run_harness.py provides BOM-tolerant input, deterministic JSONL output, atomic output/report writes, per-row agent mappings, and schema/length validation.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: The round 4 harness contains the BOM handling and the atomic writes. The frozen round 3 run_harness.py is byte-identical to the starters and contains neither; the round changes only the desktop policy. The report describes development work that the delivery does not contain. 5. repair that reaches the delivered artifact. For contrast, DeepSeek-V4-Flashs BrowseComp run M06 answers zero in the first round by finding concrete protocol mismatch: All 50 rows scored 0 with valid contracts [. . . ] missing Authorization on model/search calls (the starter sent it on all calls). The next candidate restores the header, broadens response parsing, and revises the research policy. Its development score reaches 34 and it stays selected through three further rounds. The frozen source contains the restored header, and the trajectory records local check of the whole pipeline against mock broker. Held-out performance rises from 18 to 46 (S = 34.1). This repair fixes fault the feedback exposed and reaches the delivered agent.

sections.title: J LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Repetition. The main comparison and the harness studies build each pairing of builder and task once. Native Optimization objectives vary between repeated evaluations of the same agent (Section F), so individual Optimization results carry that variation. The development-case, prompt-prior, and eight-task studies use three independent builder runs per condition and report their differences descriptively. Model-based judging. Creation and Editing Result scores are assigned by model judge (Zheng et al., 2023) that applies the task rubric to the delivered artifacts and execution traces. Validity gates and rubric ceilings bound the judges discretion, but the scores still inherit its errors. The static source assessment of Section 5.3 uses the same judge. In both judged families, the judge shares model family with at least one builder: GPT-5.6 Sol in Creation and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, beside DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, in Editing. Evaluation settings. Each task family fixes one runtime model and one judge  (Table 9)  , so absolute levels are comparable within family but not across families. The development-case, prompt-prior, and extended-budget studies use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as builder, runtime model, and judge, and the extended-budget study also changes the case budget and the requirement (Section E.2); each study is compared only within itself, not with Table 1.
